summary: This document specifies how UDPTL, the main transport used for T.38 fax, can be carried over DTLS. It also covers how this is indicated in SDP and negotiated in sessions set up with SIP.

eli5.summary: Fax messages sent over the Internet can be read by anyone along the way. This RFC explains how to wrap them in a secure envelope and how both sides agree to do it.

questions: how does t.38 fax work over dtls
subtitle: How to wrap T.38 fax packets in DTLS so fax over IP gets encryption and tamper protection, and how SDP signals it.

tldr.problem: Fax sent over IP using UDPTL travels unprotected, even though fax often carries sensitive personal, corporate and governmental data. Earlier fax security options saw little market adoption.
tldr.mechanism: A DTLS layer is placed between UDPTL and UDP, and the two endpoints agree to it through SDP using a new UDP/TLS/UDPTL proto value, a setup attribute for roles and a fingerprint attribute for certificates.
tldr.outcome: Fax gets integrity and confidentiality protection without changing UDPTL or the layers above it. RFC 7345 has since been updated by RFC 8842.

today: RFC 7345 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8842. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Secure Fax Needed a New Approach
sections.content:
Fax can carry sensitive personal, corporate and governmental information. On the old telephone network, secure fax was never widely prioritized. On IP networks, where information might be intercepted or spoofed, the RFC calls integrity and confidentiality protection for fax vital.

Two security options already existed: an application-layer scheme in Annex H of ITU-T T.30, and fax transport over RTP/SAVP in ITU-T T.38. The RFC says both had been available for many years and never gained any significant adoption. It also says T.38 over RTP accounts for a negligible percentage of fax-over-IP implementations.

The protocol that nearly all fax over IP actually uses is UDPTL, described in Section 9.1 of ITU-T T.38. So this document secures UDPTL itself, after a 3GPP study concluded that UDPTL over DTLS was the best way to get secure fax in the IP Multimedia Subsystem.
sections.eli5: Older ways to lock up faxes existed, but almost nobody used them. So this RFC locks up the kind of fax almost everybody really sends.

sections.title: UDPTL Inside a DTLS Channel
sections.content:
The design inserts one layer. The stack becomes the fax protocol on top, then UDPTL, then DTLS, then UDP, then IP. UDPTL and everything above it need no modification, and no DTLS extensions are required.

DTLS is used as specified in RFC 6347. Once the DTLS handshake has completed successfully, UDPTL packets MUST be carried in DTLS record layer application_data packets. Waiting for the handshake means no fax data is sent insecurely.

An application_data packet does not say what protocol it carries. That is why the use of a dedicated DTLS association for UDPTL has to be negotiated, using SDP and the offer/answer mechanism.
sections.eli5: The fax message goes into a locked box before being mailed. Nothing about the fax itself changes; only the box is new, and the box is not opened for sending until both sides have checked each other's keys.

sections.title: Negotiating with SDP Offer and Answer
sections.content:
Each endpoint MUST create an m= line for each UDPTL-over-DTLS stream and MUST put the value UDP/TLS/UDPTL in its proto field. The connection attribute MUST NOT be used. The setup attribute from RFC 4145 decides which side plays which DTLS role.

  • The offerer SHOULD use actpass, unless it insists on sending the DTLS ClientHello (active) or receiving it (passive). It MUST NOT use holdconn.
  • The answerer MUST answer with active or passive, never holdconn. If it is active, it MUST start the handshake by sending a ClientHello to the offerer's address and port.
  • If the offerer ends up active after reading the answer, it MUST send the ClientHello. An offerer that sent actpass or passive MUST be ready to receive a ClientHello before the answer arrives.

To change the session later, either side MAY send a new offer. The existing DTLS association can be reused if the fingerprints and transport parameters are unchanged. Otherwise a new association is created, the old one is deleted, and each endpoint must accept data on both while both are alive.
sections.eli5: Before talking, the two sides use a short note to agree who knocks first on the door. If nobody cares, the person who made the call lets the other choose.

sections.title: Certificates, Fingerprints and Cipher Suites
sections.content:
An endpoint willing to use a cipher suite with a certificate MUST include an SDP fingerprint attribute (RFC 4572). Endpoints MUST support SHA-256 for fingerprints, and SHA-256 is preferred.

UDPTL over DTLS MUST support TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. It MUST prefer the ECDHE suite and any other Perfect Forward Secrecy suites over non-PFS suites. Implementations SHOULD disable TLS-level compression.

The certificate received in the DTLS handshake MUST match the fingerprint received in SDP. If it does not, the endpoint MUST tear down the media session immediately. It may wait for the other side's fingerprint before connecting, but that can add latency.

For anonymous calls, a new self-signed certificate SHOULD be used for each call, and its attributes MUST NOT allow correlation or identification of the caller, especially subjectAltName and commonName.
sections.eli5: Each side shows an ID card and also writes a short code for it in the note. If the ID does not match the code, the call is hung up at once.

sections.title: NAT, Rekeying and Falling Back
sections.content:
With ICE (RFC 5245), connectivity checks run before the DTLS handshake. All candidate pairs for one component belong to the same DTLS association, so there is only one handshake. After an ICE restart the handshake is repeated, a new association is made and the old one is deleted.

STUN packets MUST be sent directly over UDP, not over DTLS. To tell them apart on one address and port, a first byte of 0 or 1 means STUN, and a first byte from 20 to 63 inclusive means DTLS.

During rekeying, reordered packets protected by the old keys can still arrive, so receivers MUST keep both key sets for some time. How long is out of scope.

If a user requires secure transport and the remote side lacks UDPTL over DTLS, no fax stream can be established. A user who would accept insecure fax can offer both variants using SDP Capability Negotiation, or send a new UDPTL-over-UDP offer after a rejection.
sections.eli5: Mail from different senders can reach the same mailbox, so the receiver looks at the first number on each piece to see which kind it is. If the other side cannot do locked boxes, you either give up or agree to send it unlocked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism gives integrity and confidentiality protection for fax. The usual DTLS approach is to verify a PKIX certificate against a server's domain name, but the RFC notes that issuing PKIX certificates to all clients is not realistic in most deployments.

So the design relies on the integrity of the SIP signaling instead. If each side can verify the integrity of the SDP it receives, the DTLS handshake cannot be hijacked by a man-in-the-middle. SIP Identity (RFC 4474) is given as one easy way to provide this, and S/MIME or future mechanisms could also serve.

Without such integrity protection, the security is limited to defense against passive attack by intermediaries. An active attack on the signaling plus an active attack on the media plane can attack the connection.
sections.eli5: The note that says which ID to expect must not be swapped in transit. If it is safe, nobody can sneak in; if not, the lock only stops people who are just listening.

sections.title: Example Call Flows
sections.content:
Appendix A walks through two flows between Alice and Bob. In the first, Alice sends a SIP INVITE with an SDP offer using m=image 6056 UDP/TLS/UDPTL t38, a=setup:actpass and a fingerprint of her self-signed certificate. Bob, after checking Alice's identity, sends a DTLS ClientHello directly to her and the handshake completes. Each side checks the peer certificate against the SDP fingerprint, and Bob's SIP 200 OK carries a=setup:active. After Alice's ACK, T.38 fax flows over UDPTL over DTLS.

The RFC notes that Bob need not wait for the handshake to finish before sending the answer. If he has already sent the 200 OK and later finds a fingerprint mismatch, he terminates the session.

The second flow upgrades an existing audio-only session through a re-INVITE that removes the audio stream and adds the secure fax stream, noting that this is how non-secure T.38 sessions are traditionally set up.
sections.eli5: The examples show two friends agreeing by note to use the locked box, checking each other's IDs, and then sending the fax. One example starts the fax in the middle of a phone call.
